Chapter 1: Searching for Something Real—The Longing for God in Everyday Life
Have you ever felt that quiet ache, that subtle sense that something’s missing—even when, on the outside, your life looks just fine?
Maybe it’s a restlessness that sneaks up in the middle of a busy day, or an emptiness that lingers after you hit a milestone and still don’t feel fulfilled. Sometimes, it’s a sharper longing—a deep ache that surfaces when life falls apart and nothing the world offers seems to satisfy.
That longing, even when we can’t quite name it, is where so many journeys begin—a journey that brings together faith, doubt, and the search for meaning.
In therapy, this ache shows up in all kinds of ways. Imagine a woman sitting across from her counselor, nervously twisting her hands as she tries to put words to a sadness that just won’t go away. She’s read the books, tried meditation, even turned to medication, but that heaviness still lingers. Or picture a young man who, on paper, seems to have it all together—but deep down, he feels like a fraud, haunted by the sense that his life is missing something essential.
These stories aren’t rare. If you listen closely, you’ll hear the same quiet questions echoing in countless hearts: Is there more to life than what I see? Does anyone really care? Is God out there, and if so, could He possibly care about me?
Now, for those who grew up around religion, these questions can feel even heavier. Maybe you remember praying as a kid and feeling like nobody answered. Or maybe you sat through church services that left you cold, or got burned by hypocrisy or judgment, making you want to steer clear of anything religious. But even among the skeptics, there’s often a longing for something beyond what we can touch or measure. It’s almost as if our hearts are wired to reach for the divine—even when our minds want to push it away.
In the therapy room, these aren’t just big, abstract questions—they’re deeply personal. Picture a dad, struggling with anxiety, who admits he sometimes whispers prayers when no one’s around, not sure if anyone’s even listening. Or a college student, weighed down by depression, asking if God could possibly care about someone as broken as she feels. These moments are raw and honest, and they reveal something important: beneath the pain we carry, there’s often a spiritual hunger that’s just waiting to be named.
It’s tempting to write off these longings as wishful thinking, or just the result of how we were raised. And, honestly, a lot of folks in mental health have been taught to be skeptical of spiritual experiences—sometimes seeing them as nothing more than coping mechanisms or even warning signs.
But after years of listening to people’s stories, a different picture starts to emerge. Again and again, people describe moments they can’t explain—encounters with something, or Someone, that feels loving, powerful, and unmistakably real. Sometimes it’s a breakthrough in the middle of a crisis; other times, it’s a gentle reassurance that slips quietly into an ordinary day.
Like the woman grieving her child, who talks about a deep peace that washed over her one night. She can’t put words to it, but she knows it was real. Or the man fighting addiction, who suddenly finds a strength he never knew he had. These aren’t rare, dramatic stories—they’re woven through everyday life, often hidden behind layers of doubt or shame.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: this longing for God isn’t a flaw or an illusion. It’s a core part of being human—a sign that we’re made for something more. Healing, then, isn’t just about fixing symptoms or changing habits. It’s about being open to the idea that the ache inside might be pointing toward something real. Maybe even Someone who’s closer than we ever thought possible.
